Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. 

We believe our core ideas can be adapted for other object detection and pose estimation tasks that rely on the PnP algorithm.

CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for this difficulty, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, it introduces the concept of the angle-Hausdorff metric, which it uses to offer a solution to the second of Menger's problems. This approach, presented here, differs from the one proposed by R. Englebert in 1966. The article's key findings also imply the existence of embeddings that preserve distance for certain types of metric spaces. The results discussed in the article are further validated through the analysis of example spaces. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.

Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. The accompanying appendix provides a step-by-step solution to the Schr\"{o}dinger equation for a two-level system to demonstrate the appearance of negative temperature in both microcanonical and grand canonical ensembles. The underpinning physics is also made accessible by reformulating the Hamiltonian and associated equations of motion. This approach is shown to be analogous to that employed in classical mechanics, thereby obviating any confusion that might arise from the use of complex numbers. The condition necessary for negative temperature to occur is identified and can be seen to be directly related to the position of the energy level(s) in relation to the laser beam(s). The appearance of negative temperature is not limited to a specific implementation, rather it is a general phenomenon that arises from the non-equilibrium nature of the system. The validity of the term "negative absolute temperature" is also emphasized, as it is essential to distinguish it from the term "non-equilibrium system", as the latter encompasses a broader class of systems that, in contrast to the two-level system discussed here, need not necessarily exhibit negative temperature. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive connection between the neutrino mass matrix and the dark matter density. This connection is expressed through the dark matter self-scattering cross-section, with an expected value ranging from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-3}$ barn. Furthermore, we determine the suitable parameter regions that meet the relic density requirement and ensure the stability of the dark matter. These regions are associated with two distinct neutrino mass hierarchy types: in the inverted hierarchy case, the most light neutrino mass can range from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{−1}$ eV, while in the normal hierarchy case, the sum of the light neutrino masses can range from $10^{−2}$ to $10^{−1}$ eV. In both cases, we find that the scoto-seesaw mechanism can successfully replicate the observed dark matter density with a thermal dark matter population. This model also imposes constraints on the Higgs mass matrix, particularly on the CP-even dark Higgs boson, which could be detectable at future electron-positron colliders with high luminosity. These findings emerge from a comprehensive analysis of the simplest scoto-seesaw model, which necessitates the integration of the minimal dark sector into the type-I scoto-seesaw framework.

In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse process to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct actual X-rays from synthetic ones with remarkable precision. Our model's performance was evaluated and compared to existing methods in the field through quantitative metrics derived from real X-rays and intermediate latent space representations. Furthermore, a critical aspect of medical model development was addressed - robustness testing, which revealed our model's resistance to various transformations that actual X-rays may undergo during use. Additionally, a innovative approach to evaluating the semantic similarity between real and synthetic X-rays was employed, confirming the semantic plausibility of the generated X-rays. Ultimately, our model's ability to produce a high-quality inverse process solidifies its potential for real-world healthcare applications.
